hlido_opinion.headline: Turns the computers you already own into shared desktops that you and your agents drive at the same time, each with its own cursor.
hlido_opinion.body: Most computer-use offerings rent you a sandbox and hand the agent the whole screen, which means you cannot work alongside it and you cannot use the machine you already trust. Cua inverts both. A Space is a desktop on hardware you own - a Mac, the Mac mini on the shelf, a Linux box, or your own cloud - and its remote desktop protocol separates input from the picture so you and every agent get a cursor of your own on the same desktop. The stated workflow is that you step in to make a call yourself and then hand it back, which is the right shape for work no one actually wants fully unattended. The surface is unusually specific about the parts that normally stay vague: Teleport packs an app's open tabs, profile and sign-ins into a session bundle, nothing is read until you approve, sensitive items require Touch ID, the Space verifies the bundle's SHA-256 before opening the app, and on Space images the bundle is sealed to that Space's own key so the relay cannot read it. Pre-granted permissions and pre-installed tools address the failure everyone hits in practice, which is an agent stopping at a permission dialog. The licensing is stated plainly rather than implied - Spaces is source-available under FSL-1.1-MIT while the Cua Driver and Lume are MIT - and the driver is usable on its own without Spaces, so the agent-facing layer is not hostage to the hosted product. What is not established is operating history: the named projects using it are a credibility signal, not a reliability record, and nothing on the surface bounds latency, session stability or what happens when a Space dies mid-task.

tier_rationale: STEADY (85) because the central claim - shared desktops on your own hardware with a separate cursor per participant - is stated precisely, the security handling of Teleport is described at a level a reader can check rather than asserted, pricing and limits are fully disclosed including the free tier's session and remote-hour caps, and the agent-facing driver is MIT-licensed and independently usable. Not VITAL because there is no public operating history or reliability record for the streaming layer, several Pro and Teams capabilities are labelled coming soon rather than shipped, SSO and audit export are explicitly not included yet, and the failure behaviour of a Space mid-task is undocumented - so the properties an operator would most want bounded are the ones the surface bounds least.
what_it_does_well: Runs on hardware the operator already owns - a Mac, a spare machine, or their own cloud - rather than renting a sandbox
Separates input from the video stream so a human and multiple agents each hold their own cursor on one desktop, with explicit hand-back
Describes Teleport's security handling concretely: approval before any read, Touch ID for sensitive items, SHA-256 verification of the bundle, and per-Space key sealing on Space images
Pre-grants permissions and pre-installs tools so an agent does not stall on a permission dialog - the most common practical failure in desktop automation
States licensing per component rather than in the abstract (Spaces source-available FSL-1.1-MIT; Cua Driver and Lume MIT) and lets the driver be used without Spaces
Publishes complete pricing with the real constraint named - live sessions and remote hours, with usage from the machine itself free
what_it_fails_at: No operating history, uptime record or reliability data for the streaming layer is visible on the public surface
Several paid-tier capabilities are marked coming soon (expiring share links, 90-day audit history), and SSO plus audit export are explicitly not included yet
Nothing states what happens when a Space fails mid-task - no documented recovery or session-durability behaviour
The named projects using Cua establish interest, not reliability; no case study bounds performance under load
Latency is described qualitatively (low latency over QUIC on the same network) with no published figures
best_for: Teams that want agents operating real desktop applications on machines they control rather than in a rented sandbox
Operators who need to watch an agent work and take the keyboard mid-task without killing the session
Anyone whose workflow depends on an app's existing sign-ins and profile being present rather than re-authenticating inside a fresh VM
Developers who want only the desktop-control layer - the MIT-licensed driver is usable standalone
not_recommended_for: Organisations that need SSO or exportable audit logs today - both are named as not yet included
Teams with no spare hardware and no cloud of their own, since the model assumes you bring the computers
Workloads needing a contractual uptime or latency guarantee - none is published
Anyone requiring fully unattended long-running sessions, as session-failure behaviour is undocumented
red_flags: No operating history or reliability record for the streaming layer, while the product's whole value depends on that layer holding a live desktop session
Enterprise controls a buyer would treat as table stakes (SSO, audit export) are stated as coming next and are not available

compared_to.verdict_diff: Browser-use drives a browser; Cua drives a full desktop on hardware you own, including native applications, with a separate cursor for the human. Choose browser-use for web-only automation that needs no desktop; choose Cua when the task requires native apps or an existing signed-in profile.

agent_relevance.agent_integration_path: Agent-first by design. The open-source Cua Driver lets an agent operate native desktop apps on macOS, Windows and Linux without seizing the human's cursor or keyboard, and is MIT-licensed and usable independently of the hosted Spaces product. Spaces start with permissions granted and tools installed, and a provider connected once in Connections is available to coding agents (Claude Code and Codex are named) inside every Space with nothing to configure. No MCP endpoint is advertised on the public surface.
